sections.title: A small brown bolete
sections.text: The peppery bolete (Chalciporus piperatus) has a cap usually 3–7 cm across, occasionally larger, convex at first and then expanded. Its smooth surface ranges from tawny or yellow-brown to reddish brown; it can be slightly sticky when wet and drier with age.

sections.title: Rusty pores and a yellow-based stem
sections.text: Beneath the cap, the tubes run slightly down the stem. The angular pores, fairly broad for a small bolete, are yellow-brown when young and then become cinnamon, rusty or reddish brown; they turn brown when handled and do not typically stain blue. The slender stem is ringless and lacks a reticulate network, often similar in colour to the cap, with vivid yellow mycelium at its base. The flesh is cream to yellowish, more distinctly yellow at the stem base; the spore print is cinnamon brown.

sections.title: Among trees from summer to autumn
sections.text: This mycorrhizal fungus occurs in woodland near broadleaf trees such as birch, beech and oak, and also with conifers, including pine. Records vary by region. It fruits mainly from summer to autumn, though dates depend on the local climate.

sections.title: Taste and food safety
sections.text: Its flesh tastes strongly peppery. Culinary opinions vary, and the German Society for Mycology reports gastrointestinal symptoms after consumption in larger quantities. Some sources mention using it sparingly as a seasoning, but that is not a recommendation to eat it. Chalciporus pseudopiperatus is very similar; yellower pores that bruise blue may point to that species, but reliable identification can require molecular analysis.

traits: Small cap, usually 3–7 cm, convex then expanded, tawny to reddish brown
Slightly decurrent tubes; angular cinnamon to rusty-brown pores that turn brown when handled and do not typically blue
Slender brownish to yellowish stem, without a ring or reticulation; vivid yellow mycelium at the base
Cream to yellowish flesh, vivid yellow at the stem base; strongly peppery taste
Cinnamon-brown spore print; mycorrhizal with broadleaf and conifer trees, mainly fruiting from summer to autumn
Digestive symptoms have been reported after eating larger quantities; a close relative can be difficult to distinguish
safetyNote: Do not treat it as a routine edible mushroom: its taste is strongly peppery, and the German Society for Mycology reports gastrointestinal symptoms after consumption in larger quantities. Uses as a seasoning mentioned by some guides do not establish safety. Do not taste or eat a wild specimen without expert identification.
